opening.headline: Average usage is within limits, but during peak periods for a few minutes, errors occur in a service. We'll explore methods to pre-allocate capacity and plan accordingly.
body: Operating an internal AI assistant, you'll find that daily average usage falls far short of its limit, yet requests are rejected during specific time periods. Retrying requests may reduce errors, but response times become slower. This happens because the limit responds to peak instantaneous usage, not average usage.

In this class, we first examine what limits quotas and allocations impose, and in what units. Then, we compare reserved capacity as described in Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic documentation using the same framework, and verify numerically how committed amounts cover usage. Finally, we discuss a case where baseline capacity is reserved and peak demand is handled on an on-demand basis.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the concepts of reservation throughput and allocation volume.
Traffic conditions that require reservation and those that do not can be distinguished.

screens.title: Limits and delays occur simultaneously during peak hours.
screens.lead: First, read about common scenarios encountered while operating services. Consider what might be wrong by reviewing the following error examples.

visual.alt: In the daily 24-hour request volume curve, only the peak period in Monday morning exceeds the threshold, with error response cards placed below it in the diagram.

paragraphs: On Monday morning at 9 a.m., a large number of requests accumulate from internal assistants. Some calls return a `429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` error. However, when viewed over the entire day, the average utilization remains well within the limit. Reaching the limit occurs only for a few minutes during peak periods.

The reason is that limits are measured across multiple axes. The Gemini API documentation describes limits along three axes: requests per minute (RPM), tokens per minute (TPM), and requests per day (RPD). Usage is compared separately against each limit, and an error occurs if any one of them is exceeded. Even if there is headroom available for TPM, if the RPM limit is 20, any request beyond the 21st per minute will be rejected.

What happens if we increase retries? Denied requests keep coming, leading to longer delays, and users perceive the service as slow. While documentation recommends waiting a moment before resending or reducing call frequency, this only alleviates the symptoms without increasing capacity.

callout.label: Questions to be answered in this class
callout.text: How can we pre-secure capacity that remains stable even at peak loads, and how much capacity should we pre-secure?

screens.outro: First, let us recall what this situation looks like in your service.

screens.title: Recall the peak capacity utilization rate of our service
screens.lead: After first thinking through each question on your own, selecting an answer allows the instructor's thought process to be revealed. There is no requirement to input or submit an answer, and neither correctness nor incorrectness is evaluated.

items.prompt: Do you know up to what percentage of utilization rate during peak hours can be reached?
items.answer: Many teams only look at average usage. This causes them to miss when their limits are reached. Limits react to peak instantaneous values, so usage should be evaluated based on the busiest period, not the average.

items.prompt: Is the quota project-based or organization-based?
items.answer: It varies by provider. The Gemini API documentation states that limits are applied at the project level rather than per API key, while the Claude API applies limits at the organizational level. You need to understand at which level usage is aggregated in order to determine whether multiple services share a single limit.

items.prompt: Is the first limit the request count or the token count?
items.answer: When there are many short requests, the request volume tends to reach the limit first; when there are many requests involving long documents, the token count tends to reach the limit first. The response behavior depends on which limit is reached first, so it's essential to first understand the shape of your traffic.

items.prompt: What is displayed on the user screen when the limit is reached?
items.answer: Typically, slow responses or error messages are observed. By working backward from the symptoms the user experiences, it becomes easier to distinguish between capacity issues and design problems.

screens.outro: We will now examine the key concepts required to answer this question in sequence.

screens.title: Quota and allocation specify what is limited and in what unit.
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms highlighted below, a brief definition appears. Please review each term one by one.

data.text: The Gemini API measures quotas along the RPM, TPM, and RPD axes on a project basis, and daily quotas are reset at midnight in Pacific time. Quotas vary based on usage tiers and ascend to higher tiers as expenditure increases. In addition, there is a per-minute expenditure-based quota. The Claude API applies quotas at the organization level and defines them by usage tier, with each tier having its own Monthly expenditure cap. The Claude API manages quotas using a Token bucket model, meaning capacity is not reset in fixed intervals but instead continuously accumulates, which can lead to errors during brief spikes in demand. Quotas are Maximum allowable value and do not represent guaranteed minimum capacity. Quotas set at the organization and workspace levels can be read as Rate Limits API.

terms.tip: This is the request count. It counts only the number of requests, regardless of the size of each request.
The number of tokens input per request. Services that frequently send long documents may reach this limit before exceeding the request count.
This is the daily request count. The Gemini API resets to zero at midnight Pacific Time.
This method continuously fills at a constant rate. Since it does not get fully initialized at a specific time, brief congestion spikes could potentially reach capacity limits.
There is a monthly cost cap defined per tier in the Claude API. Once the cap is reached, usage is suspended until the following month's beginning, and responses of 429 are returned.
This means there is a limit that one must not exceed. It does not mean that sufficient capacity is always guaranteed.
An API that reads the limits set for organizations and workspaces programmatically. It can be used to align the gateway's settings with the actual limits.

screens.outro: If the limit is merely an upper bound, then there is a need for a separate method to pre-allocate capacity. Let's compare the reservation methods of the three providers using the same framework.

screens.title: Compare reservation throughput within the same framework
screens.lead: Select each tab to review the reservation methods by provider. All tabs are structured in order of what is being purchased, unit, overage, and applicable scope.

visual.alt: A diagram showing that the reservation mechanisms of the three providers share a common structure consisting of basic load provisioning and cap-and-quotas for excess.

tabs.label: Google
tabs.body:
**What are you buying?** Provisioned Throughput is a fixed-cost, fixed-term subscription. You reserve throughput for the supported models.

**Unit.** You specify the model and the location where the model runs to reserve capacity. The duration can be selected from various options, with fixed pricing on a monthly or weekly basis.

**Overage.** The throughput allocation document divides capacity reservation into two methods: a pay-as-you-go model and a fixed-price model. The pay-as-you-go model includes Standard, Priority, and Flex.

**Scope.** Consider this for real-time production apps such as chatbots and agents that require consistently high throughput, a consistent user experience, and critical cost control.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body:
**What are you purchasing?** Reserved Tier is a product that allows Enterprise customers to pre-purchase the throughput of a specific model.

**Unit:** It is displayed in dollars per minute ($/min). The document explains that using dollar units makes it easier to estimate how much is needed.

**Overage:** Usage exceeding the reserved amount is billed at the standard consumption-based rate.

**Scope:** Reserved capacity is added to the existing rate limit. It can be flexibly used across all context lengths and regions for Standard and Fast modes, but does not apply to Batch or Flex usage.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body:
**What is being purchased?** This document describes limits based on usage tiers rather than purchasing capacity separately. Tiers are automatically determined based on usage history, and users can request an upgrade if higher capacity is needed.

**Unit:** Limits at the organization level, with the option to set per-workspace user-defined limits. Each tier has a monthly spending cap.

**Overage:** When usage exceeds the limit, a 429 response is returned. Once the spending cap is reached, usage is suspended until the following month.

**Scope:** Current settings can be verified via the Rate Limits API. All limits are maximum allowable values, not guaranteed minimums.

screens.outro: The common structure involves pre-allocating capacity for baseline loads and sending excess demand on a metered basis. Let's examine how this structure operates in terms of cost using numerical examples.

screens.title: Agreement and overage: billed based on covering usage with reservation amounts
screens.lead: When reviewing the example from the OpenAI documentation where $2 per minute is reserved, check the table to see how usage over a 12-minute period is handled. Pay special attention to cases that exceed the reservation limit.

data.notes: Usage is calculated based on a tiered rate. For durations such as 6 minutes, 7 minutes, or 8 minutes that exceed $2, only the excess amount beyond $2 is charged at the standard rate, and the request is not rejected. Instead, an agreement includes a fee. For durations like 1 minute or 12 minutes, even with low usage, the reserved amount remains unchanged. Therefore, reservation size is typically aligned with baseline load rather than average or maximum usage. In the table, only three instances exceed the reservation line at 12 minutes, and the total excess charge amounts to $1.25. Also remember that if the service does not consume $2 continuously throughout the 12-minute period, the entire reservation fee is not fully depleted per minute. Understanding this cost structure is essential for determining the appropriate reservation fee.

screens.title: Explanation: Always-on baseline is reserved, peak is on-demand

steps.title: Verify the example
steps.body: A hypothetical internal support chatbot receives consistent requests during off-peak hours and experiences short spikes at Monday mornings and month-end. The question is: how much to book, and how to handle the remainder?

steps.title: Find the base load line
steps.body: Let's look at the hourly usage distribution for one month. The baseline load is almost always above this level. We examine the distribution rather than the daily average because the limit responds to the instantaneous peak.

steps.title: Reserve up to the basic line
steps.body: We set the reserved capacity to the base load. We do not align it with peak maximum values because even though the peak duration is short, the reservation cost continues to be incurred during idle periods.

steps.title: Overflow sections are sent in batch quantities.
steps.body: Segments exceeding the baseline are charged on a volumetric basis. Usage exceeding reserved amounts is billed at standard rates, so service is not interrupted. Costs only increase during peak periods.

steps.title: Checks the limit of the fixed-quantity section
steps.body: Even in sections transitioned to a capped model, you might reach the general limit. Check your usage tier and request an increase in limit if needed. Reservations and limits are separate entities.

steps.title: First, determine the model and location.
steps.body: Reservations are specified at the model level, and in Google's case down to the location, so you must first determine which model and region to use. You cannot assume that changing the model will automatically apply the reservation to the new model.

screens.outro: We will examine how the reservation size affects the results.

screens.title: Explanation: How does changing the reservation size affect things?
screens.lead: Move the slider to try small, medium, and large reservation sizes, and compare how cost predictability and utilization differ under the same load.

stops.body: The reservation cost is low. However, usage typically exceeds the reserved capacity and is charged on a volumetric basis. Cost predictability is poor, and when overage reaches a threshold, delays or errors may occur. This makes the reservation option largely ineffective.

The base load is stabilized by reservation, with only brief peaks managed on a demand-based basis. The utilization rate relative to reservations remains high, minimizing waste. This is the recommended approach. Since excess demand occurs only for short durations, cost volatility is low and planning is straightforward. However, if rare events such as end-of-month spikes affect service quality, the capacity limits of the demand-based tier should also be reviewed.

Book enough capacity to cover peak demand. While quality is most stable, usage during off-peak times remains at the same cost, resulting in low utilization. The longer the peak period, the higher the waste ratio. When the agreement period is long, it's also important to consider that this waste continues throughout the entire period.

screens.outro: I will conclude by organizing three decision criteria. First, whether the actual usage rate closely matches the reserved capacity. Second, whether excess capacity causes delays or errors that impact service quality. Third, whether the scale can be adjusted after the agreement period ends. Together, these three criteria provide a basis for determining whether to set a conservative or more expansive scale.

screens.title: Summary: Basic provisioning is stabilized by reservation.
screens.lead: Now, let's summarize and organize the content we've reviewed so far. Read the three paragraphs below in sequence to verify the key points.

paragraphs: The limit is not a guarantee but a ceiling. An error occurs if any of the metrics such as RPM, TPM, or RPD is exceeded, and the system responds to sudden spikes in load. Therefore, you cannot simply conclude that capacity is sufficient based on average usage alone.

Reservation capacity is a separate purchasing method that pre-allocates resources to resolve this issue. Usage exceeding reserved allocations is charged at a tiered rate, per model and location. In some cases, such as with OpenAI's Reserved Tier, this does not apply to Batch or Flex usage, so it is important to verify what is covered.

The core of design is scale. It involves sizing based on baseline load rather than peak load, continuously monitoring utilization, and jointly defining the paths and limits for excess capacity. By stabilizing baseline demand through reservations and offloading spikes on an on-demand basis—as demonstrated in this course's example—both cost predictability and service stability can be achieved.

glossary.def: This is a purchasing model that reserves a certain throughput level by specifying a model and location. Google's Provisioned Throughput and OpenAI's Reserved Tier fall under this category.
This is a fixed-cost, fixed-term subscription provided by Google. You specify a model and location to reserve processing capacity.
RPM, TPM, RPD are limits on the volume allowed within a specific time period. These limits vary depending on the usage tier and do not represent guaranteed capacity.
This is a contract form where a fixed amount of capacity is agreed upon for a specified period, resulting in costs being incurred even during periods of low usage.

misconceptions.myth: Increasing the limit is like a reservation.
misconceptions.fact: The limit is merely the maximum allowed amount and does not guarantee capacity. Reservations are a separate purchasing method that pre-allocates capacity.

misconceptions.myth: Reservations must be made in proportion to peak size to ensure safety.
misconceptions.fact: Usage exceeding reservations is handled on a volumetric basis, so the service will not be interrupted. To avoid wasting costs during off-peak times, it is typical to scale according to baseline load.

misconceptions.myth: When reserved, all request types are overridden.
misconceptions.fact: OpenAI's Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex usage and is billed on a pay-as-you-go basis. You should verify what is included in the reserved tier in the documentation.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The limit is not a guarantee but an upper bound, and an error occurs as soon as any one axis exceeds it.
Reservation throughput is calculated per model and location, and any excess is handled under a volumetric fee.
Reserve size should be based on baseline load rather than peak load, and usage rate should be continuously monitored.
